questions.stem: Nineteenth-century novelists routinely claimed the privileges of an {1} narrator, entering any character's private thoughts at will; Flaubert, by contrast, often confined himself to what a merely {2} observer, stationed in the corner of the room, could have inferred from a gesture or a glance.
questions.explanation: The first blank names the narrator's unlimited access to interior life, which is omniscience, not many-sidedness (multifaceted) or mere conspicuousness (remarkable). The second blank needs the human limit case — someone who only sees, but sees finely — so keen in its sense of acutely perceptive; avid would describe the observer's appetite rather than the sharpness of his perception, and versatile his range of skills, neither of which is what inference from a gesture requires.

questions.stem: Retired from the bench at seventy, Justice Rowan became a {1} gardener, spending more hours in her greenhouse than she had ever spent in chambers.
questions.explanation: The hours logged in the greenhouse establish enthusiasm, and keen and avid are the two words that make the sentence report exactly that — keen in its everyday British sense of leaning forward, avid a shade hungrier but equivalent here. Methodical and desultory both attach naturally to a gardener and are grammatically faultless, but they describe how she works rather than how much she wants to, and desultory flatly contradicts the evidence of the clause.

questions.stem: The priest's graveside eulogy was measured and brief; only when the coffin was lowered did the older women of the townland begin to {1}, in a high, sustained, wordless cry that the visiting folklorist later transcribed as music rather than speech.
questions.explanation: Set against the priest's measured speech, the blank must name loud ritual wailing over the dead, which is the verb keen — a homograph wholly unrelated to the adjective meaning sharp or eager. Intone would make the sound a level chant rather than a high rising cry, and elegize means to compose a formal poem of mourning, an act of controlled authorship rather than vocal abandon.

questions.stem: Early accounts reduced the famine to a single cause, the failure of one crop, but the commission's report insisted that the catastrophe had been {1}, tracing it to tenure law, export policy and administrative doctrine at once; what was {2} was less any one of these findings than the willingness of a government body to indict itself.
questions.explanation: The list of three simultaneous causes forces multifaceted, the word for many-sidedness treated as real structure; monolithic asserts the single cause the commission rejected. The second blank must mark what compels comment — a self-indicting official report — and remarkable does that coolly, whereas incidental would call it minor and plausible would rate its credibility, neither of which the concessive comparison supports.

questions.stem: Paul Robeson resists the single label that biographers reach for: he was a {1} figure — trained lawyer, All-American athlete, concert bass, and lifelong campaigner — and no account that fixes on one of these survives contact with the others.
questions.explanation: The catalogue of unrelated careers, plus the warning against fixing on one, calls for many-sidedness, and multifaceted and versatile are the two options that deliver it. Controversial and indefatigable are both true of Robeson and read smoothly in the slot, but neither is entailed by a list of distinct talents, and resourceful praises ingenuity under constraint rather than breadth.

questions.stem: Brilliant and insufferable, the young editor conducted himself as though he were {1}: he met every correction with a pained smile, as if the point had merely slipped his mind rather than been news to him.
questions.explanation: The joke in the second clause is that he cannot admit being told anything new, which is the posture of one who claims to know everything already — omniscient, used here in its mocking application to a human being. Erudite would credit him with learning acquired by effort, and shrewd implies calculation and angles, which is precisely the flavour the sentence does not have.

questions.stem: For an administration that had campaigned on fiscal discipline, the budget displayed a {1} indifference to arithmetic, projecting revenues that no forecaster outside the party was willing to endorse.
questions.explanation: The opening contrast between the campaign promise and the budget makes the indifference conspicuous enough to compel comment, and remarkable and striking are the pair that say so — remarkable runs in reverse like this, attaching to failures as readily as to feats. Feigned and habitual sit comfortably in the slot and are individually plausible of a government, but one makes the indifference a pretence and the other makes it routine, which drains the contrast the sentence has just set up.

questions.stem: Hazlitt's prose is {1} in the older sense of the word — an edge rather than an ornament, drawn across whatever it touches — and it is therefore {2} that so cutting a writer should have been, in company, the mildest and most easily wounded of men.
questions.explanation: The gloss "an edge rather than an ornament" fixes the first blank as sharpness, the original sense of keen, which covers blades, frosts and minds alike; multifaceted would praise range and omniscient knowledge, neither of them a matter of edge. The second blank then depends on the first: because the prose is cutting and the man was mild, the contrast draws comment, so remarkable — while inevitable and unsurprising would deny the very incongruity the sentence builds.
